did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with the heading “A Psalm of Asaph” and presents an image of God standing in the divine assembly and judging among them.
Did you know? Rather than immediately describing the injustice, the psalmist addresses the judges with a pointed question: “How long?” This emphasizes that ongoing injustice demands an answer.
Did you know? The command “Defend the weak and the fatherless” teaches that biblical justice includes a special responsibility toward the vulnerable, including the poor and the orphan.

Did you know? Alongside fair judgment, practical rescue is also required: “Rescue the weak and the needy from the hand of the wicked.” The psalm connects the pronouncement of judgment with protecting those who have been harmed.
Did you know? The judges’ failure is portrayed not merely as a personal moral problem but as a danger to the whole society: “All the foundations of the earth are shaken.”

Did you know? This verse says, “You are gods,” referring to the “sons of the Most High.” In the context of the psalm, the title emphasizes their exalted status and responsibility to judge justly; it does not grant them immunity.

Did you know? Immediately after describing the judges’ exalted status comes a sharp reminder of their limitations: “You will die like mere mortals”—even those who hold authority will die like human beings.
Did you know? The conclusion, “Rise up, O God, judge the earth,” turns the psalm from a rebuke of human judges into a prayer that God judge the whole earth, “for all the nations belong to you.”
